title: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: adding more dimensions does not ultimately seem to have much effect on the occurrence of behavior of any significant complexity.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Cellular Automata” (from p. 170), p. 170. Scope: simple programs (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems) in one, two and three dimensions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large bounded spaces can be simulated now and give informative comparisons. No sampling scheme or dataset covers all simple programs, and conclusions depend on encoding and complexity definitions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Construct matched rule ensembles in one, two, and three dimensions for specified formalisms, classify behavior with common complexity measures, and compare prevalence and attainable classes. Similar rates support dimension-independence within those ensembles; large systematic differences refute it there.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The scope spans several infinite formalism classes.

Fundamentally change and significant complexity are vague.

Rule ensembles across dimensions are not canonically comparable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.62
data existence: 0.82
operationalizability: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.5
discriminating power: 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: One-dimensional elementary cellular automata are fully enumerable, and two-dimensional totalistic rules are searchable with public software, so a dimension comparison is a real computation. Three-dimensional samples and the words 'does not fundamentally change' keep the result from covering the whole claim. The test can detect a gross dimension effect and cannot certify that no such effect exists outside the sampled families.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For matched families of cellular automata, Turing machines, and substitution systems in one, two, and three dimensions, estimate the fraction of small rules with irregular behavior. A sharp drop or jump in that fraction with dimension would challenge 'does not fundamentally change'; stable fractions would support it inside those families.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Three-dimensional and large-neighborhood rule spaces can only be sampled, and the sample can miss rare complex rules.

'Fundamentally' and 'not much effect' move with the classifier and with how rules are paired across dimensions.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.6
